In view of the fact that family allowances are, by law, universal and without a means test and, further, that a survey is now being conducted by Statistics Canada into the personal habits and incomes of every twenty-eighth recipient of family allowances and, further, that those interviewed are told that they must respond to these questions by an interviewer under penalty of a fine or imprisonment of up to three months, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Halton-Wentworth (Mr. Kempling):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have discussed this matter often. These organizations are not borrowing as much at this time because there is a great deal of liquidity in Canada. The savings rate for the third year in a row is at a record level.
Because we are having this balance of payments problem, we must maintain some inflow of capital. We have borrowed in order to achieve this, and as we are operating the exchange market through the Bank of Canada, of course, it is serving that purpose at the same time.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question of privilege relates to the availability, or lack of availability, to be more accurate, of the document tabled in this House on January 25, known as the report of the Task Force on Canadian Unity. I was able to confirm-and I apologize that I was only able to confirm this just before question period because there was some uncertainty about it-that one copy only of this document will be made available to members of parlia-

January 31, 1979
Privilege-Mr. Jarvis
ment. I hasten to point out, however, that any Canadian can purchase the document for $3.50 from the Department of Supply and Services, as is the case with many government documents.
I make no comment about the content of the document. That was dealt with by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) and others on the day it was tabled. I might say that the style and readability of the document is attractive to me, and I think it is to most members. I should like to deal with what led up to the document, however. The order in council establishing the terms of reference of the commission directs that the commissioners shall, among other things;
(c) contribute to the knowledge and general awareness of the public the initiatives and views of the commissioners concerning Canadian unity;
The first line of the report indicates that the task force was created:
-with a broad mandate to obtain and to publicize the views of Canadians regarding the state of their country-
I emphasize the word "publicize", Mr. Speaker.
Finally, if I may quote briefly from the Prime Minister's remarks on January 25, he said, as reported at page 2552 of Hansard:
I am confident the report will take its place as a document of the first importance-
Later, he had this to say:
I am sure that all members of the House, all members of the provincial legislatures, and many thousands of Canadians will want to read and reflect carefully on this report.
I find myself in the unusual position of agreeing, without reservation or qualification, with the Prime Minister in terms of that particular statement. We have a document about which we may conclude there is no doubt of its importance, no doubt of the mandate the commissioners had to publicize their findings and, finally, there is no doubt, on no less an authority than the Prime Minister, that thousands of Canadians want to read the report.
How does that affect my rights and privileges, given the situation where only one copy is available to me? First of all, I must ask myself why I have the rights and privileges in the first place, and why I share them with fellow members. I believe that part of the reason is to enable me to fulfil the responsibilities that the electorate has bestowed upon me. Whether one interprets those as a quasi-trust relationship, a particular political mandate or not, I believe I have certain responsibilities. Given that position I believe that certain rights and privileges are accorded me in order to fulfil those responsibilities. One tool-whether it be important or unimportant is purely subjective in the mind of a member-is documentary material.
I should like to refer to a situation which I believe to be completely analogous. It was not long ago that certain constitutional proposals were put before us. In relating that to my specific riding, I wish to inform you that in the usual course through an annual questionnaire I consult my constituents on

various issues. I was told through my last questionnaire-and I suspected this to be the case-that 82 per cent of my constituents who replied did not regard the constitution as a high priority compared to other issues, namely, the economy. An even larger number, 85 per cent, indicated that they wanted more access to constitutional information. I do not consider those results contradictory, Mr. Speaker. In the minds of constituents, one reason for establishing the priority may be the lack of information. I interpreted those results in terms of my responsibilities to mean that I had an obligation to get as much information to my constituents on that issue as was possible.
As a result of this I-and I am sure many other members have done so-consulted the information service that provided the constitutional material. I received crates of material, Mr. Speaker. It was piled almost to the ceiling of my office. My staff was intimidated by the quantity. I did my best, and was able to distribute about 2,000 copies of this package which was composed of five documents. I am sure many other members were faced with the same situation. We were literally barricaded from our offices by the stacks of material.
Relating that case to the task force, I got only one copy of that report. Maybe I could accept the proposition that my rights and privileges can be changed, can be lessened or ameliorated, given certain other higher priorities. I think restraint of government spending is not a bad argument for changing certain rights and privileges from time to time, particularly in terms of documentary material. I can accept that. I may argue about whether the government should pick that particular document in order to exercise restraint, but I would accept it as a pretty good argument that it wants to cut costs.
How can I accept that it is the restraint on spending that prevents me from getting more than one copy of the unity report on the one hand when, on the other hand, I deal almost daily with the Canadian Unity Information office through the Department of the Secretary of State and in one package alone I received 41 documents? The initial package contained 41 individual documents-posters, pamphlets, booklets-now I can even get phonograph records. I can get them by the thousands and tens of thousands from this office, dealing with exactly the same issue as that dealt with by the task force.
When I can get tens of thousands of copies of gun control documents, tens of thousands of budget documents-even tens of thousands of the speeches of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan)-

The House resumed from Tuesday, January 30, 1979, consideration of the motion of Mr. Lalonde (for Mr. Reid) that Bill C-9, respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last night, when I called it ten o'clock, I was saying that Canadians generally do not want a referendum on the constitution, that generally they are not particularly concerned about the constitution. What the majority of Canadians want is a sound administration in which the unemployed can find work, the mother of a family can have something to put in the refrigerator, as I said last night. Mr. Speaker, let us not make a secret of the fact that, since 1976, since the Parti Quebecois came into power, we have heard all sorts of statements on national unity from men in the public eye.
In the last three years, we have been able to see that such statements, instead of creating harmony and allowing citizens from the various parts of Canada to better understand one
80047-3 3'/2

January 31, 1979
Referenda
another, has fostered discord between provincial and federal governments. From what 1 have seen in the last few months, there is a fight going on between the two main parties involved in this constitutional conflict, namely the Quebec premier and the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau). One of my fellow-citizens pointed out to me recently, speaking of the constitution and the deadlock and disagreements between the Quebec and central governments, that they reminded him of two roosters fighting over the same hen, not to meet the needs of and satisfy the hen, but to gratify their pride and vanity.
So, Mr. Speaker, those two, with their resounding statements, are only aggravating the debate. They are only stirring up more discord between the two governments instead of finding, or attempting to find, ways of appeasing those divergent views. No, Mr. Speaker, it is neither with referendums nor with meaningless speeches that we will find a way to get along together. It is very simply through considerable understanding, by making allowances, even many allowances, and by everyone doing his or her part that we can achieve harmony from the Pacific to the Atlantic.
Mr. Speaker, so long as the federal government is not assuming its responsibilities and placing monetary creations under the responsibility of the Bank of Canada instead of the chartered banks, we shall face problems of this nature. As a matter of fact, we shall only be able to live in harmony in Canada when we all have something to put on our table, when we all have the feeling to live in a beautiful and great country, and are sure that tomorrow will be full of promise for each and every one of us. So I hope, Mr. Speaker, that this government will at last assume its responsibilities and give us assurances in that regard.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I could certainly not refrain from making some comments in this debate on second reading of Bill C-9. I have already heard several speeches, and I may tell you immediately that I do not agree with everything I have heard in the House on this legislation.
Yesterday, I heard members from Quebec, and particularly the Minister of Communications (Mrs. Sauve), who urged the hon. members of the House to support the government in its endeavour to acquire this repressive tool because she felt the danger which is upon us. I was sorry to see her lack of trust in the decision that Quebeckers will be making, and I think that she has acknowledged her party's failure to satisfy the legitimate aspirations of a province and meet with the objectives of a majority of Quebeckers as well as of all Canadians, who would want to see, in this constitutional reform, a chance to secure an interesting future for all concerned.
I also heard, one of our colleagues, a member from the NDP, say how surprised he was to see that only the member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey), Quebec's representative, would vote against this bill. 1 think that our Social Credit colleagues are also aware of the dangers of this legislation and

of the government's intentions in this regard, and it is because of these intentions, which concern us, of course, and which explain the present mistrust towards this government, that our Quebec colleagues from the Social Credit Party of Canada will, I think, vote against this legislation.
But I think we must first of all try to find the reason for introducing this national legislation on referenda. It is clear, as the Minister of Communications has indicated, that the federal government, in view of Quebec's upcoming referendum, considers it essentiel to pass an act to oppose a possible decision by a majority of Quebeckers. It is obvious that the government has failed, with its Quebec team, and because of this monumental failure in the eyes of Quebeckers, who had expected a government that would have better understood their aspirations, it is trying to give itself a tool which will only lead to the worse confrontation ever.
We, on this side of the House, are confident that with a philosophy that would be concerned with Canadian and Quebec interests as well and should there be a new government, it would be possible to bring about a constitutional reform and to discuss openly a new distribution of powers thus allowing a large majority of Quebeckers to understand that philosophy and the necessity for those changes. The referendum does not frighten us at all because we are confident that Quebeckers in their wisdom and with the necessary degree of flexibility, would reject that idea of breaking away from Canada provided a federal government would come up with those changes that are necessary to meet the natural aspirations not only of the people of Quebec but also the people in various regions and various provinces.
So why that referendum in Quebec in the first place? I think it is important to remind our colleagues in this House, and on both sides, that in this country, because there has been a lot of talk in the past few days about this legislation-and I intend as a Quebecker to remind them also of a few things that might not be the most pleasant-but I don't think I will be saying anything new if I talk about the frustrations that Francophones felt in this country, even long before the Parti Quebe-cois came to power.
I am thinking, for example, of the bitter fight that was fought on a bilingual currency, on simultaneous translation, frustrations that members understand today, but how many Quebeckers came to this place without being able to be understood because there was no simultaneous translation. And bilingual currency. You will say it is symbolic. That was important years ago. Of course, things have improved and people demand more, and that is normal, Mr. Speaker, but those frustrations that were being felt by French-speaking minorities generated, particularly in Quebec, a loss of faith in the federal government and a feeling of alienation towards it.

Of course, the people in Quebec who were living in a vacuum had to put up with the situation, and their governments fought the federal government in the name of autonomy. In the last years, from 1950 to 1960, there was some improvement as some provincial ministers felt the need to co-operate with the then prime minister. But for practical purposes, let us go back to 1960 when Mr. Jean Lesage became leader in the province of Quebec as an Ottawa-trained federalist and sold the slogan "Maitres chez nous".
At that time, as my colleagues from Quebec will remember, this contributed to develop a certain awareness among Quebeckers. And, of course, Mr. Lesage sold that slogan "Maitres chez nous." He also made thousands of Quebeckers aware of that objective which was not one of separation but rather a certain concept of autonomy and nationalism which was very well received. But even Mr. Lesage did not succeed in awakening the Canadian nation as a whole and particularly his federal colleagues. In 1966, Mr. Johnson became Quebec premier and nobody will deny, I think, that Mr. Johnson, a true federalist, tried to promote the development of the Francophone bloc in Quebec while respecting the rights of the minority that had and still has its place in Quebec.
And Mr. Johnson in order to reawaken the public and make the federal government realize that changes were urgently needed had to launch the slogan "Equality or Independence". Certainly it was never in Mr. Johnson's mind, and I knew him well, to separate Canada. But he must have been really disappointed and frustrated to add the possibility of independence to his drive for equality. Mr. Johnson was after equal opportunities, equal language status, and also probably a sizeable number of jobs in the public service for Francophones I think the hon. member for Levis (Mr. Guay) knows what I am referring to and he no doubt agreed on gradual entry into the public service of a percentage of the French-speaking population.
We all know the untimely death of Mr. Johnson led to a Liberal government under Mr. Bourassa coming to power in 1970. But then again Mr. Bourassa was compelled to refer to cultural sovereignty, something that gave Liberal members here a good laugh. I remember all the humiliations that Mr. Bourassa had to suffer because of this government even though they were political cousins. This government took credit for the election of Mr. Bourassa, and because of that he could not make any decisions for himself, everything was decided by this government.

This deception in the minds of Canadians is due to the fact that there is a problem. The government thinks that it can put an end to the controversy on national unity by means of a national law on referenda. But this government does not understand that it will be unable to restore links, links of genuine friendship between all groups that make up this country unless it makes them all feel that they really participate in the life of the country, unless it gives them decent incomes, unless it makes the different groups that form the country respect each other.
All that is needed, Mr. Speaker, are changes in attitude, and openness of mind from both French and English-speaking Canadians and all ethnic groups. I suggest that we must demonstrate understanding. Realizing that it has failed the province of Quebec, that its great team has not succeeded in making room for Quebeckers within Canada, which would be acceptable to them, this government has introduced a referendum bill in the hope of offsetting the decision the people of Quebec will make in a few months from now.
Mr. Speaker, the important point is to agree to a change of attitude, commit ourselves to an early study of the Pepin-Rob-erts commission recommendations and implementation of the proposed reform, and let the provinces know just how much change is required to meet what I regard as fundamental needs and I am not thinking only of Quebec, as that province is not the only one which is dissatisfied with the present system.
There have been federal-provincial conferences which readily revealed disaffection and confrontation as between provinces, and their refusal to accept this government's attitude. So, Mr. Speaker, the lack of response with regard to the Canadian feeling, the lack of solution with respect to constitutional reform, the fact that our provincial partners have been

kept waiting for too long and the fact that our provincial premiers have been continuously confronted and treated like school children, all that has caused division in this country.
The country is facing serious questions and Canadians are concerned. Now we are asked to provide parliament with a legislation which according to government members would be the solution to the national unity problem. But how blind can they be to believe that this legislation will solve the problem? How blind and how devoid of ideas can they be to ingenuously imagine that this legislation on referenda will solve the problem in the event of a favourable answer to the referendum on sovereignty association as advocated by the Parti Quebecois, by the government of Quebec?
Yesterday, the Minister of Communications said in fact that she was concerned, and this was quite obvious, over the possibility that the Quebec government might win the referendum on its stated objective, and that we should pass this legislation as quickly as possible in order to provide the government with a tool, which would change nothing. Let Quebec decide. Do we really believe that by passing legislation on the referendum we would settle the issue? Absolutely not. I think it is high time we understood the feelings of Quebeckers and the frustrations of other provinces over other issues and that we try to resolve these problems. This national referendum bill is in my opinion nothing more than a political gadget.
The Prime Minister, in the wake of his fiasco and monumental failure on the political and economic fronts, has designed this tool to enhance his image as the great saviour of confederation. Actually he is responsible for and the originator of our present problems with his team riding his coattails and not daring to speak up. I was told yesterday that we were free to support the bill or not. That is a joke, Mr. Speaker, since we know fully well that no living body on the other side would dare stand up and speak against this legislation even if he felt like it. It was the same thing with the sales tax and with Bill C-14. We are all aware of the position, of the state of subjection of those people, and we are also aware of the deep frustrations of Quebeckers.
Today, as a Quebecker, I enumerate those frustrations we have suffered, when we are still waiting for a federal government which fails to understand what changes are needed in order to create the climate we want. Quebeckers are only too willing to find ways of improving our beautiful country of Canada. Nobody will have me say otherwise. We will immediately be accused of sleeping with the separatists. This is the argument of the weak, Mr. Speaker. They will even say, as they did last summer with regard to the sales tax, that we just wanted the vote of the Parti Quebecois members, whereas the Liberal and UN leaders supported Mr. Parizeau's position. Howe Institute issued this morning which says that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Chretien) should have copied some of the measures adopted by the Quebec minister of finance. speechtext:
It gives me great pleasure, of course, to take part in the debate on the referendum bill introduced by the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lalonde) and the Minister of State for Federal-Provincial Relations (Mr. Reid). I listened with great interest to the speech made earlier by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard). I admired the serenity with which he managed to make his point. I listened with no less interest but perhaps a little less admiration to the kind of speech that was just made by the hon. member for Joliette (Mr. La Salle), and in his case serenity yielded naturally to passion, and we know what happens in such cases. The hon. member is quite prepared to make all sorts of accusations in this House, and right after making such irrational remarks, he does not hesitate to leave rather hastily.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that in a place like this honest and upright politicians can have different opinions on fundamental positions that may affect the future of their country. What is wrong, Mr. Speaker, is that we are told half-truths and given a

January 31, 1979
Referenda
very personal interpretation of past history disguised as the truth. This is just about what he did-maybe not on purpose, maybe he simply got carried away in certain parts of his speech, but this is what he did. I would like to give a few examples of this.
He said for instance that for the government, the referendum bill is the answer to the national unity problem. No member of this House can seriously suggest that this bill was introduced for that reason. On the contrary, we have all seen, at least in the last ten years, the constitutional reform process introduced by the government, a whole series of federal-provincial conferences, and more recently, the introduction of a series of working papers prepared by the government starting with a very serious paper entitled "A time for action", as well as the establishment of the Pepin-Robarts task force which has just issued its report. The hon. member for Joliette knows quite well that it would be more honest to admit that this is not the answer of the government on the unity issue. He is well aware of the position of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau), the leader of the government, to the effect that everything is negotiable during constitutional discussions, except for two requirements, that is the preservation of the Canadian federation-and I would like to know if the hon. member for Joliette agrees with the basic principle which says that the legislatures have certain responsibilities within their respective and largely independent jurisdictions-and we all know the second requirement, Mr. Speaker, which is that basic individual rights be included in a charter which will be enshrined in the Canadian constitution.
And on that score, the political group to which the hon. member belongs certainly has no lesson to teach people on this side of the House. He only has to ask the leaders of other Conservative parties in other provinces, the hon. Premier of Manitoba or the hon. Premier of Ontario, whether they are prepared to grant the minorities who speak the other official language in their provinces the same rights granted to the English-speaking minority in the province of Quebec. He should ask them that question before giving us a lecture here.
On this side, our position cannot be more specific and straightforward. We think that all Canadian citizens must enjoy the same fundamental rights across this country which is called Canada. If the hon. member cannot make the same statement, then he has no lesson to give to the people sitting on this side of the House. According to the hon. member, the Pepin-Robarts commission stated that over the years the Trudeau government made mistakes and that it criticized the government policy. He knows quite well and I could quote from the report where the Pepin-Robarts commission gave its unqualified support to the official language policy of this government. I found another point-not very clear I must say-in the passionate address of my friend from Joliette. He also referred to the Laurendeau-Dunton commission and stated that it had not been acted upon. In other words, that report tabled by the commissioners according to him would have simply been shelved. Here again, the hon. member for

Joliette knows better than that. And I challenge him to prove me wrong. He was in this House when the government introduced the Official Languages Act which was a direct result of the Laurendeau-Dunton report.
The hon. member has the right, the privilege and even the duty to disagree with the government. But in expressing his opinions he does not have to misrepresent the stands put forward over the years by this side of the House. Besides, Mr. Speaker, we witness here one of the shortcomings of our parliamentary system, in the sense that all along opposition members took a negative stand, always taking the opposite view of that taken by the government.
Still there is a field where I think it would be extremely useful for hon. members to extend their policies and their views. As an example I take the field of external affairs where we do manage to show some sort of common front in the House; even if we do not agree on all points and all incidents that may occur from month to month and year to year, it clearly demonstrates that our position is quite similar. And, Mr. Speaker, unless federalist forces in Canada succeed in the short term in adopting a position acceptable to the majority of federalist forces, I think they will serve the interests of the Parti Quebecois which knows full well that for electoral purposes the major political groups of the country will contradict one another. The only winners in that process, Mr. Speaker, are those who want to destroy rather than build the country. And I readily recognize that the hon. member for Joliette, in spite of the half truths he said in the House of Commons, is in fact a true Canadian who wants to build a country which will be even better than it is today, which will be all the more capable of answering the needs of regions and reflecting the duality of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I had no intention to make a partisan or an impassioned speech this afternoon. Rather I intended to pursue one or two of the ideas voiced by the hon. member for Joliette. And I agree with him when he says that the rub of the debate is the phenomenon of alienation and the lack of confidence in our democratic institutions in Canada. I agree with him on this but I do entertain many reservations about his suggestions so far. I for one would like to concentrate on the question of the lack of confidence in our democratic institutions and the alienation of the people and see how the new legislation on referenda proposed by the Minister of Justice might help to a certain extent. I am not saying it is a cure-all, nobody says so, but it would help to strengthen our institutions.
Any question about the integration of the principle of referendums in our system of parliamentary democracy requires that one look fully into the meaning of the concept of democracy in a modern society. It also requires a certain assessment of the state of that democracy. The very concept of democracy, as everyone knows, has changed with the times. The concept of democracy in a modern society has certainly evolved a great deal since antiquity when it was considered as an active, continuing, personal and direct participation of the citizens in the political decision-making process. Representa-
January 31, 1979

tive democracy has replaced direct democracy, if it ever actually existed. This representative democracy is now generally recognized as the only true practical form of political government. It means that the people agree to entrust their sovereignty to a selected group of individuals to whom they have confered the mandate of governing for a limited period of time.
Today, the principle of representative democracy is widely supported by the people. Yet, according to certain studies, it seems that this support is becoming less unconditional. Some feel that a shift is taking place whereby our institutions are perceived in some circles as becoming less and less democratic. In my opinion, it is true that our democracies are experiencing problems the importance of which must not be underestimated. Some years ago, a research group submitted a report on the governability of modern democracies to the trilateral commission. The title of that report was "The Crisis of Democracy". And in their account of the situation, the authors stressed the potential dangers that threaten democratic governments. I should like, Mr. Speaker, to quote one or two extracts from that document. The authors, for instance, quoted a well-known German politician, Mr. Willy Brandt, who at the time of his resignation or shortly after, said the following:
Western Europe has only 20 or 30 more years of democracy left in it; after that it will slide, engineless and rudderless, under the surrounding sea of dictatorship, and whether the dictation comes from a politburo or a junta will not make that much difference.

Closer to home, Mr. Leon Dion, in his book La societe el la politique, la vie des groupes, wrote the following:
It has never been easy to govern. Leaders and governments nowadays are just as good and perhaps even better than they were before. Their task is often even more demanding, as the paths of democracy are more difficult today. We are entering an era where literally everything is in question. This is a challenge and we must meet it.
These views may seem pessimistic although they want to be realistic, but they bring the problem in a perspective of urgency. We have to ask ourselves questions about the condition of our democracies, either here in Canada or elsewhere, about their viability in the future, and about the means which would ensure their continuity in the future. In the case of Canada, it is up to us and we cannot shirk the problem.
Some people will insist that there is no such emergency at least as far as our country is concerned. They will point to the strong participation rate of the electorate-80 per cent-a typically Canadian phenomenon. It seems to me that if we want to assess correctly the health of our democracy we must examine the question further. One of the revealing factors in that respect is the degree of political alienation of a society. In the case of Canada, in spite of some studies made in that area, this phenomenon is still not very well known. However, the few indications there are point to a few conclusions. Political
Referenda
alienation must be examined at two different levels, the individual and the group.
As far as the individual is concerned, a number of studies in Canada clearly show that people are indifferent to politics. Here in parliament we see only people for whom political life is everything. This is the centre of political life in this country, the place where we hear criticism, the place where major political decisions are taken but, of course, that high level of interest is not found everywhere across the land. The indifference rate is generally estimated at 50 per cent of the people, and more troubling still, those studies also point to a definite feeling of being powerless in the face of politics. Some 45 per cent of the people believe they have little or no influence on political events. In a democratic society, these results deserve to be closely studied by those who are interested in political life in a democratic context.
Although it is difficult to statistically evaluate how these attitudes change in time, it appears that despite higher schooling, which is usually recognized as a factor of increasing participation in political life, a significant part of the people remain indifferent to politics. If we look at political knowledge among Canadians, results confirm the foregoing conclusions. We are faced with a population that has little concern for politics unless it affects their daily lives. For instance, Mr. Speaker, three months after the general election in 1965, a Canadian survey showed that 25 per cent of the people could not identify their member of parliament, 15 per cent could not identify his party and, more important, 58 per cent said they had read or heard nothing about him.
Another survey among 1,000 university students showed in 1973 that while 98 per cent could identify the prime minister and the governor general, 3 per cent only could identify the Speaker of the House of Commons. And we all know, Mr. Speaker, that according to a fairly recent Gallup poll, very few Canadians can even name one federal cabinet minister. I quote, in English, from the October 28, 1978 Gallup report.
When Canadians were asked recently to name a cabinet member in Ottawa, and to identify his responsibility, 33 per cent were able to supply this information correctly. Another 14 per cent recalled the name of a cabinet minister but were unable to identify or incorrectly identified his responsibility. This compares to 19 per cent who named someone other than a present-day cabinet minister, and to 34 per cent who would not venture a guess.

It would be possible, Mr. Speaker, to support these facts with other examples. Of course, some people will now say that democracy is protected by the existence of a solid and well-established party system which guarantees the possibility of enlightened choice. Unfortunately, once again we cannot be too optimistic. More and more surveys show a continuous erosion of the party identification phenomenon. Thus people are less and less inclined to identify themselves with a political

party. The allegiance of individuals has become short-lived, and now, from election to election, more and more citizens change their allegiance, going from one party to the other. I refer now to a survey sponsored by the Gallup firm which was published in La Presse of January 16, 1979. We read the following comment:
At the beginning of December, a Gallup poll showed that 21 per cent of Canadians are tied to a political party; 7 per cent are very committed; 14 per cent, more or less. Another 22 per cent of the adult population can be classified as sympathizing. Most voters, 55 per cent, reject any connection with a political party.
As for the phenomenon of political alienation, at the community level in Canada it is especially felt through regionalism and the task force directed by Messrs. Pepin and Robarts has given a detailed description of that phenomenon. We often hear about the alienation of western Canada toward eastern Canada. We should also include among those phenomena of political alienation the separatist movement in Quebec and probably also the isolation feeling in the Atlantic provinces. In each case there is a deep feeling of under-representation in relation to the real weight and such feeling leads to the disparagement of political institutions in Canada.
Needless to say, that political alienation does exert strong pressures on our institutions. Indeed those pressures are so strong that they even threaten the survival of Canada. Both kinds of political alienation to which we have just referred put Canada in a paradoxical situation which is even dangerous in a certain sense. On the one hand, we are witnessing a lack of political interest and involvement on the part of an important sector of the Canadian population, and as a result a considerable loss of support for our political institutions. Here again, Messrs. Pepin and Robarts pointed out this phenomenon in a very interesting fashion. On the other hand, increasing pressures are being brought to bear upon those very same institutions, even in Canada. In this connection, I should like to quote from the findings of the trilateral commission in its book "The Crisis of Democracy" which deals with Canada. One can read these conclusions, and I quote:

As identified by this colloquium, Canada's foremost governability problems can be regarded as falling within four major areas: the questionable ability of the evolving political institutions to aggregate an increasing volume of demands efficiently and at the same time to retain their accountability to the public; the increasing rhetoric/performance gap; the decline of a 'public philosophy'; and the problem of communications. Several characteristics of the Canadian system were found actually to enhance Canada's governability, that is, its parliamentary and federal structures of government, a reasonable degree of decentralization of authority and the absence of class-based political parties. However, a general consensus emerged that Canada's governability problems (as redefined) while not insoluble are real and deserve urgent attention and remedial action.

In short, we are being told that our political system has been well served by political decentralization by our parliamentary system and by the absence of events generating a loss of confidence, such as the one the Americans lived through,

which culminated in the removal from office of the President of the United States.
However, those characteristics, and others as well, are not solutions to the problem; at the very most, they could serve as checks on a growing tendency. It is therefore imperative for us to consider what remedial measures can prevent that tendency from becoming a permanent reality and completely undermining our political system.
We are now discussing the possibility of making the referendum one of our political institutions. We should take advantage of this opportunity to think of that instrument in terms of the revalorization of our parliamentary democracy. Indeed that is the aspect I would like to deal with in the rest of my remarks.
In my opinion, the referendum can constitute a positive means in the context of a more extensive democratization of our institutions. It might enable us to bring closer the government and the people, a move which our system seems to need badly.
As we all know, referendums are used in numerous countries. One thinks immediately of Switzerland, the United States, France and now, of course, Great Britain. In each case it would be possible to show that the institutionalization of this means of popular consultation was brought about by a clearly felt need to associate the people with some very important political decisions. In all cases representative democracy was associated with the concept of direct participation by the people in the decision-making process. Depending on the countries and the needs involved, the use of the referendum has developed unevenly. Some, like the United States, have deemed it advisable to make an extensive use of it, while others have been satisfied with a more restricted use.
Some hon. members have said that the idea of a referendum may not be consistent with our British-type parliamentarian-ism. In my opinion, they are wrong. However, although there may not be an opposition between the two ideas, I think a certain incompatibility may develop in connection with the use of the referendum. For instance, an excessive use of it would not be in agreement with the principles of a British-type parliamentarianism which are essentially based on the sovereignty of parliament.
It goes without saying that like any other instruments, referenda offer not only advantages, and that an abuse of them may bring about disadvantages which may exceed by far their advantages. It is necessary to realize that a referendum will not remedy all the ills of our democracy. Although it is an extremely useful tool of democracy, it will not solve the problem of political division. As far as Canada is concerned, we must never lose sight of this principle. An excessive use of referenda can also result in a downgrading of the role of politicians and undermine the principles of representative
January 31, 1979

democracy. The most positive aspect of referenda is that it provides an opportunity for grass root involvement in major political decisions requiring a long term commitment. By the same token, it can bring about a sense of belonging in the national community by enhancing the value of political institutions and creating a feeling of genuine participation in the hearts and minds of ordinary citizens. As far as upgrading the image of our political institutions is concerned, I would like to make a suggestion regarding Bill C-9.
Pursuant to clause 1 of the bill only the governor in council may direct the Chief Electoral Officer to issue writs for a referendum. No other person, group or agency has this authority. Accordingly, the government has decided on a government-initiated referendum, implicitly rejecting a parliament or people-initiated referendum. I think that the popular referendum used in some U.S. states does not suit parliamentary democracy and that its serious disadvantages would prevent its use in our parliamentary context.
However, I am not at all convinced, Mr. Speaker, that the same arguments can apply to the parliamentary referendum. It is a principle of government which is recognized in several countries, in Denmark for example. The parliamentary referendum could revitalize parliamentary institutions. The conditions would be subject to discussion and we could easily conceive that could come before the House in committee of the whole following a proposal by two-thirds of the hon. members. This procedure is not at all incompatible with the government-initiated referendum and it would favour the development of a more important role both for the elected representatives and for the people.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say that in the next few months, perhaps particularly in the debates on matters affecting national unity, we could try to move further and further away from those ad hominem attacks which make perhaps the fame of what happens in the House of Commons to take a much more positive attitude and to demonstrate clearly and precisely our positions and to try to sell them to the Canadian people not because they are taken by a particular individual but rather because they meet the deep aspirations of the population and because they will bring about changes which will benefit the people who elected us. Furthermore, the basic principle which should never be left aside is that individuals should come before governments, that governments are here to serve the individuals and not the other way round.

This blinkered approach to a strong Canada is evident in the commitment of the Leader of the Conservative party to do away with Petro-Canada, our national oil company, which in a few short months succeeded in bringing back under Canadian control an important percentage of our hydrocarbon industry.
Why do Conservatives want to do away with Petro-Canada? Partly the reason is ideological: pure free enterprisers do not want the government around, even if it means turning around a situation in which more than 85 per cent of the Canadian

petroleum industry was foreign owned. According to this line of reasoning, it is all right if companies such as Petro Par, controlled by the Government of France, or BP, controlled by the government of Great Britain, can own a major chunk of our oil resources; but it is not all right if we Canadians do it through our government. As I have said, it is only partly ideology which has driven the Conservative party to a commitment to abolish Petro-Canada. The other driving force in this commitment is the regionalism to which the Conservative party now is catering. In simple terms, some westerners do not want a national oil company in their resource field.
Let us look at the Yukon. The Conservative party now is committed to giving provincehood to the Yukon. What does that mean? It means provincehood to the Northwest Territories shortly after, and eventually it means turning over the natural resources of the Yukon and the Northwest Territories to extremely small populations. That policy was enunciated by the Leader of the Opposition and the Conservative party. If that is the position of the Conservative party, the Liberal position is somewhat different. The government considers the natural resources of the north are the common heritage of all Canadians. First and foremost, the inhabitants of the north should call upon those resources to assure themselves a standard of living second to none in Canada. But after that occurs they are the heritage of all Canadians, and they are part of the cement which can bind and can continue to bind the country together.
What is the position of the Conservative party on offshore resources? In effect the Leader of the Opposition wants a turnover of offshore resources to the provinces. The 600,000 square miles which have been added to the Canadian sovereignty are a Canadian heritage; they belong to all of us. In effect, the position of the Conservative party will give these to the provinces.
What will happen to the things required to attract Canadians to a strong central government, if these two policies of giving away our Arctic and offshore resources-

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR HOLDING OF REFERENDUMS ON CONSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to address myself for a few minutes to this notorious Bill C-9. Several of my colleagues have already spoken, and still others will because this bill is of great interest to us. I also note, Mr. Speaker, that this bill on referenda is being debated after the publication of the Pepin-Robarts report, which is a direct consequence of the election of the Parti Quebecois, and also after the decision, taken by Quebec, to hold its own referendum. As the hon. member for Champlain (Mr. Matte) said a moment ago, I am convinced, Mr. Speaker, that if Quebec had not decided on a referendum, we would never have discussed the issue in this House.
It is always the same thing, I mean the reason for all this bickering, the main reason for all this bickering in the House and across Canada, the fact that the government is not doing its job and is always jumping on the back of the provinces, especially of Quebec. I think that we will have to say things clearly in the future and state whatever is on our minds.
Some people say: Quebeckers are impulsive people. But I was glad to see, in the course of the debate, that there are impulsive people among English Canadians too. I used to think English Canadians were so cool that they had no reactions at
Referenda
all, but they do react as soon as you interfere with their rights. As the preceding speaker just said, if you meddle with the rights of English Canadians in Quebec, we will react, we will rise and we will fight. I congratulate them for such a noble stand, but let them realize that for 111 years, Quebec has respected the rights of English-speaking Canadians and for 111 years, these same rights have been denied to Frenchspeaking Canadians in the other provinces.
I think that French-speaking Canadians outside Quebec- and the hon. member tells me that they agree about that- have been extremely patient. Therefore, we can understand that they are more exacting in the stand they take today. I think English-speaking Canadians should try to understand them instead of bullying them. But I do not wish to develop that point any further since it is not the issue I want to addresss myself to today. Others have talked about that and it serves no purpose to start all over again.
I would like to add a few words to whatever has been said and call attention to the remarks of the previous speaker because deep inside I was pleased having finally realized that English-speaking Canadians are like any other people; when they feel threatened and think they are discriminated against, they can react.
Well, Quebeckers have been reacting for 15 years. I hope that that turning point in history will enable us to restore a sound measure of fairness. Mr. Speaker, the government is now ready to deal with an important issue which concerns the fate of all Canadians. In the interpretative clause 2 of this bill, the following definition was maintained:
"Constitution of Canada" includes, without limiting the meaning of that expression,
(a)	the customs, conventions and enactments that comprise the Constitution of Canada, and
(b)	the political and judicial institutions and processes of Canada;
That interpretation, Mr. Speaker, is too broad. The government is running the risk of needlessly thrusting its designs and constitutional concepts upon the provinces.
In fact, this definition is so unprecise that it would permit parliament to interfere more and more in provincial affairs by bringing the majority party into play. This bill would make it possible to seek the approval of all Canadians or some of them on all agreements and settlements relating to constitutional matters. Thus it would become the ideal tool for federal intervention into provincial jurisdictions by merely allowing voters all over Canada to negate provincial decisions. This policy would in fact deny provinces their sovereignty. Let us take a look at the confederation act, or read the definition of a confederation in a dictionary: We will find it is the union of sovereign provinces.
Today, it is no longer possible to mention sovereignty, or claim our province is sovereign under confederation without

January 31, 1979
Referenda
being branded a separatist. Provincial legislative assemblies have received a very precise mandate from the voters whom they represent directly, to the same extent as federal members. Members of provincial legislatures appear to belong to a lower category. Well, no, Mr. Speaker. The purpose of this bill is to do away with the concept that the federal government must act as the co-ordinator of the provinces, the creation on a more or less voluntary basis of a separate political and economic entity, made up of the British colonies joined together. The British North America Act distributed the powers in a precise way, leaving to a central government the responsibility for legislating on behalf of all parties involved certain questions of common interest.
The time-honored customs and agreements of jurisprudence determine to a large extent the current and future destiny of Canada. Under Bill C-9, the federal governement could hold a referendum to make significant changes to these agreements. Since we all know that the present cabinet is not too keen on provincial demands for amendments to the constitution, these consultations of the Canadian public may serve as a means to bypass provincial legislatures, this stratagem has been used in the past and may very well be used again in the future.
We still remember the conscription during the 1939-45 war, Mr. Speaker. We did not forget it. They held an election on that, and it was also under a Liberal administration which said: They will never force conscription upon us. Then they attracted lower Quebec that way, and they knew that Quebec was 95 per cent against that conscription. Well, they established it from coast to coast, and we were cleaned out but we were not forgotten because 4,000 of our young people were killed in the slaughter, in battlefields, as our French Canadians were used to protect the British troops which were behind them.
Mr. Speaker, we do not want such situations to recur through a referendum. Now we are told: Yes, but we shall have a 40-hour debate when we move a motion for a referendum. And the hon. member who spoke before me said earlier: It will have to be accepted by both Houses. Fine. But we know that with the system we have today, when the government takes a decision, with compulsory vote for all its members, sure enough, the legislation is passed. Even if you fight for 40, 50 or 80 hours, it will pass. It does not matter any more.
There is also to some extent some danger with regard to the independence of the highest judicial system in our country. In fact, Bill C-9 would authorize the government to interfere with the decisions made by the Supreme Court of Canada or by appeal courts. This is what could happen. An appeals court making a decision in favour of a province might prompt the government to exercise its right to hold referendums so as to challenge this decision through the electorate. This legal precedent would put into question the whole judicial infrastructure which protects the judiciary system against all political attacks

from within or without, from within if the institution becomes a political organization, and from without if the institution is the victim of political attacks. Any government interference in the judicial process would be extremely prejudicial to the independence of our courts of justice.
Those remarks might seem excessive, Mr. Speaker, but they serve to make a very important point in the debate. This bill refers only briefly to the type of circumstances that would prompt the government to hold a referendum. The bill only provides that the governor in council has the responsibility to hold a referendum. The decision is made at the ministerial level.
If the department considers that an issue related to the Constitution of Canada or any amendment thereto it requires the opinion of the electorate, the governor in council may, by proclamation, order that it be put through a referendum to the electorate of Canada or of any province mentioned in the proclamation. Besides, such is the intention now as concerns the province of Quebec.
The circumstances in which a referendum is required are not specified at all. Yet, it seems to us normal and even inevitable that the government should take legislative action to clearly define the requirements for holding a referendum. And only through strict regulations will abuse of discretion be avoided. It is therefore important to make sure that the government will bring forward specific criteria so as to prevent any political group from misusing such a tool.
This referendum bill allows the federal government to hold a referendum within a province, many provinces or across Canada. However, it does not elaborate on instances where a referendum may be held in any area in Canada. The government should define more clearly that clause of the bill so that public opinion will not eventually be manipulated.
Since the bill empowers the cabinet to determine the scope of the referendum, the government might exploit interregional antagonisms in this country to get the results it wants. The bill as worded would allow the government to take away, through devious means, the right to participate of a province expected to fiercely oppose the referendum. This is a possibility since the bill does not say how the government would determine the provincial or national scope of the referendum.
For this reason, the referendum, because of a reactionary hurry motivated by the Quebec referendum formula, may become a political instrument with which the federal government could materially alter the desires of the federated components.
One of the most often repeated points in the verbal struggle launched in the House of Commons on the referendum issue revolves around the fact that the House of Commons could always defend public interest during the period of debate reserved for members under clause 3 of the bill. The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby (Mr. Broadbent) had this to say:
January 31, 1979

"If there is a particular referendum which we do not think is popular, the point is that we have the means in this House as an opposition to hold things up beyond the eight days. Indeed, if it happened that the government of the day, whether it be this government or any other, rammed through a referendum bill in the face of united opposition in the House of Commons, one does not have to guess what would happen. A referendum of that nature which did not have reasonable support and had to be rammed through would be defeated in advance. Any government would know that."
I am not at all as sure as that, Mr. Speaker, because I can assure you that in the 17 years I have been in the House, every time the government wanted to pass a law there was nothing to prevent them from doing so. They have all the means to have it passed. We believe that the common position of the Liberals and of the New Democratic Party shows a definite lack of perspective. There are very rarely unanimous votes in the House. Following the directives of the caucus of the two main political parties, we have to realize that there will always be an important division in the House on serious legislative measures. In other words the present parliamentary structures are such that unanimity in the House is very rare indeed.
The hon. member for Oshawa-Whitby and his friends show a certain amount of dishonesty when they foresee the possibility of a consensus between the cabinet and the federal members. On the contrary, the current political make-up of the House would lead one to believe that on any controversial questions about the referendum there would be a division. If need be a majority government could easily get a motion passed explaining the proposed referendum to this House without serious clashes unless it clearly perceived the unpopular character of that motion among a majority of voters. The electoral vote is always what they fear.
The title of Bill C-9, an act respecting public referendums in Canada on questions relating to the Constitution of Canada, makes it quite obvious that if Quebec had not decided to hold a referendum within its boundaries in order to find out the opinion of Quebeckers about a major issue in that province, the central government would never have thought of presenting such a bill. It therefore demonstrates to the people that the federal government can no longer take the initiative because Quebec is always one step ahead. The federal government therefore keeps playing its dangerous game of hide and seek. As soon as Quebec takes a step forward in its struggle for liberation and survival, the federal government comes right after him making the same move in all sectors. When it comes to examples there are plenty of them available. As soon as Quebec opens new fields of taxation, the federal government grabs them. The latest example and the least funny is that of Loto Canada where it got in in order to make unfair competition to the provinces. There would be no end to the list of such interventions if I wanted to state them one after the other.
Referenda
As soon as they saw that the provinces were making a little money with Loto Quebec, Loto Ontario, etc., they established Loto Canada, and it is like that in every area. And then, Mr. Speaker, they are hypocritically surprised at the present crisis. They are even looking for the causes. I would say that the only cause of that crisis is the ever increasingly centralistic attitude of the central government in the hope that some day it might turn the provinces into simple administrative areas, a solution that Quebec will never accept, and the Prime Minister knows it quite well.
The Prime Minister once said here in this place that the federal government had no business in the bedrooms of the people; I believe the time has come for him to put his theory into practice and to get out once and for all of the bedroom of the province of Quebec before Quebeckers take it upon themselves to get him out in their own way in the next general election. As I said before sincere and loyal Quebeckers are jealous of their sovereignty that is guaranteed under the BNA Act, and in spite of the hundreds of repeated violations by the central government, they will not allow federalists to go and snoop in their province, which is their exclusive jurisdiction.
After being harassed for 111 years without hope for more understanding, Quebeckers are reluctant and we should not wonder why. Therefore I believe that because of the present form and intended purpose of Bill C-9 our party cannot accept it and we are going to vote against it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Rober-val (Mr. Gauthier) for the excellent speech he has just given and for the stand he took on this bill. In 17 years of parliamentary life he certainly has seen a great number of bills, but I wonder: has he ever seen a bill designed to achieve as negative a purpose as Bill C-9? The government, the Liberal party, avowedly introduced this bill to counter the Parti Quebecois, a party elected democratically within a province by people who, I think, decided they had had enough, a party which may advocate the separation of Quebec, and does decidedly advocate the right of the province to determine its fate, and which also advocates, I feel, through that right to determine its fate, the giving back to all the provinces of Canada the powers that are rightfully theirs under our Canadian constitution.
I note that this bill will lead exactly to the same type of confrontation that occurred at the time of the two Canadian plebiscites. I have here the figures on the plebiscite on the Canadian conscription held on April 27, 1942; they prove the spirit of confrontation it stirred.
In that plebescite, 25 per cent of Quebeckers voted for conscription, and 75 per cent against, while in the provinces other than Quebec the ratio was practically the opposite: 80 per cent of the people in English-speaking provinces were for conscription and 20 per cent against. It led to a state of

January 31, 1979
Referenda
confrontation at that time, a state of uneasiness and abdication in a country.
This bill will probably create the same situation: confrontation between French and English-speaking Canadians, even though they could live in harmony and respect each other if we had better laws. The hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Lambert) often talks about harmony and I believe it is a good term to describe Canadian unity. Harmony is unity of thought and 1 believe that the Canadian people can achieve this.
Bill C-9 is rather long. It contains many clauses. One thing that strikes me about this bill is that it authorizes a referendum to be held at the same time as a provincial election or referendum since it says that a national referendum cannot be held at the same time as a federal election. Why such a restriction? Why do we need twice as many expenses? Why not hold a referendum at the same time as a federal election? Why not hold one during a provincial election? Once again, this simply aims at creating confrontation with the provinces.
Quebec could decide to hold an election tomorrow morning and the federal government could say: As we cannot get openly involved in this election, we shall do so indirectly. We shall get involved in the election by holding a referendum at the same time. This is quite legal. We could hold a referendum at the same time as the referendum in Quebec. The bill allows this.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Moreover, because of this bill, confrontation will continue. I should like to give an example which everybody can understand. Suppose the Supreme Court of Canada, dealing with Quebec Bill 101, decides that a particular section is acceptable under the Constitution. The federal government, refusing to accept this decision, decides to submit the same question to the opinion of the Canadian public in order to have it judged and reversed.
With this bill, we also run the risk of weakening the judiciary and letting the political power interfere with the judiciary. As a matter of fact the federal government, namely the Liberal party, is trying to impose its will on the provinces and to deprive them more and more of their sovereignty. The powers of the provinces have been eroded since 1968 and even before. The federal government is entering more and more into areas of provincial jurisdiction. A spirit of confrontation is brought about and a little sovereignty is taken from the provinces. This bill will enable the government to go further into the provincial fields of jurisdiction and to take a little more power from each of the provinces of Canada. The spirit of sovereignty does not exist only in Quebec, but also in most provinces which want to have what belongs to them under our Canadian Constitution which is not implemented, which is eroded quietly, day after day, with some little piece of legislation and then another little piece of legislation. Furthermore, the federal government increasingly takes hold of cultural fields, taxation and other fields. Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock?
